575.title: Through a glass (1 Corinthians 13:8–13)
575.hook: now we see through a glass darkly, then face to face
575.howItsDone: Catholics speak of the beatific vision, the sight of God face to face, as the final hope of the Christian life; the Church teaches the saints in heaven already enjoy it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, charity, and Paul's list of what it does. Your line was one breath longer.

Turn off a phone in a dark room and look at the black screen. You can see your face, sort of: a shape, shadows where the eyes are. That's close to what a mirror gave you in Corinth. Mirrors then were polished metal, and even a good one showed a dim, slightly wobbly face. Paul has just said that charity never falls away. Now he explains why almost everything else will: right now, even the wisest person is looking at a reflection.
screen: `A FACE IN A BLACK SCREEN.` → `METAL MIRRORS IN CORINTH.` → `EVERYTHING ELSE WILL PASS.`

segments.voice: Prophecies will end, he says. Tongues will cease. Knowledge will be destroyed. We know in part and we prophesy in part, and when that which is perfect comes, the partial will be done away. Then two pictures. Growing up: when I was a child, I spoke and thought like a child, and when I became a man I put away the things of a child. And the mirror: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known." The Greek behind in a dark manner is a phrase meaning in a riddle, and that word, ainigma, is where English gets enigma. So, in Paul's picture, faith isn't blind. It sees something real, but indirectly, the way one works out a riddle. Look at the end of the verse, too: even as I am known. Paul's hope isn't only that he'll finally understand God. He is already fully known, and will one day know in the same way. The Church calls that final seeing the beatific vision; the Catechism says the saints in heaven see God face to face, as he is, and that this is the happiness of heaven. Then Paul closes the chapter: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Why the greatest? Thomas Aquinas gives an answer: face to face, no one needs faith in what can't be seen, or hope for what's already given. Charity is the one that doesn't end.

segments.voice: Think of something you can't figure out right now: why something happened, what comes next, what God is doing, if you believe in God. Don't try to solve it; picture it as a face in an old metal mirror, really there but blurred, and let it stay blurred while you breathe. If you pray, hand it over with Paul's words, now I know in part; if not, let the not-knowing sit beside you without fighting it.

576.title: Where is thy sting (1 Corinthians 15:51–57)
576.hook: O death, where is thy victory
576.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dying, and the Church offers the anointing of the sick and Viaticum, a last Communion; 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings for a Catholic funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, enigma: seeing now in a dark manner, and the hope of seeing face to face. Your line was then, face to face.

Some people in Corinth had decided the dead don't rise. Souls might go on, they thought, but bodies? Bodies rot. Paul answers them in chapter fifteen, and it's an argument most of the way through: he reasons, lists the people who saw the risen Christ, talks about seeds and harvest. Then, near the end, the argument turns into something more like a song. He starts taunting death itself, as if it were a bully that's finally been beaten.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `PAUL ANSWERS IN CHAPTER FIFTEEN.` → `AN ARGUMENT TURNS INTO A SONG.`

segments.voice: He begins with a secret: "Behold, I tell you a mystery." Then the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin Vulgate, reads: "We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed." Bibles translated from the Greek put it the other way round: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. The copies of the letter differ here, and translators follow the text they have. Either way, Paul's point stands: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible. Then he borrows from the prophet Hosea and makes it a dare: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" The Greek for sting is kentron: the stinger of a bee or a scorpion, and also the goad a farmer used to drive an ox. Paul names the stinger: the sting of death is sin. Preachers sometimes add a picture: a bee that stings once leaves its stinger behind. In that picture, death stung Christ, and lost its sting. And Paul doesn't end with a final argument. He ends with thanks: "But thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Catholics hear this chapter at funerals and confess it every Sunday in the Creed: I look forward to the resurrection of the dead. The Church never pretends death doesn't hurt. A few verses earlier, Paul himself calls death an enemy, the last one to be destroyed. An enemy, but a beaten one.

If you pray, use your own words, or the Hail Mary, which asks Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death. If you don't, wish them peace.

577.title: Earthen vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7)
577.howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments act by the power of Christ, not by the worthiness of the minister (ex opere operato), which is often explained with this verse in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kentron: the sting Paul asked death about, before giving thanks for the victory. Your line was death, where is thy sting.

In the winter of 1946 to 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd threw a stone into a cave above the Dead Sea and heard something break. Inside were tall clay jars, and inside the jars, rolled scrolls: some of the oldest copies of the Hebrew scriptures ever found. Plain pots, the kind any household had, had kept them safe for nearly two thousand years. Paul never saw those jars. But writing to Corinth, he reached for the same picture to describe himself and every Christian: treasure, kept in clay.
screen: `A STONE THROWN INTO A CAVE.` → `SCROLLS IN PLAIN CLAY JARS.` → `TREASURE, KEPT IN CLAY.`

segments.voice: Just before today's verse, Paul has been talking about light: the God who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts. Then he says what holds that light: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us." The Greek word for earthen means plain baked clay, the stuff of ordinary pots and cheap oil lamps. Corinth made clay lamps by the thousand, and some scholars think Paul has a lamp in mind: a cheap clay shell with a flame inside. Why would God choose clay? Paul answers in the same verse: so it's obvious where the power comes from. The Corinthians were impressed by polished speakers, and some of them found Paul unimpressive. His answer isn't to polish himself up. It's to point at the cracks. In the next lines he lists them: pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. The clay takes the blows. The treasure stays. Catholics hear something of their own teaching here. The Church holds that the sacraments don't depend on the holiness of the priest who celebrates them: Christ acts in them, through the minister. The priest is clay. So is every bishop, every parent teaching a child the sign of the cross, every tired volunteer. That's not an excuse for carelessness. It's a kind of relief: the treasure was never theirs to begin with.
screen: `LIGHT OUT OF DARKNESS.` · `EARTHEN: PLAIN BAKED CLAY.` · `PRESSED, BUT NOT CRUSHED.` · `THE SACRAMENTS DON'T DEPEND ON THE PRIEST.` · then, large: `WE HAVE THIS TREASURE IN EARTHEN VESSELS.`

segments.voice: Pick up a mug or a ceramic bowl, or cup your empty hands as if holding one, and feel its weight, the rough base, maybe a chip on the rim you've stopped noticing. Hold it gently, the way you'd hold something that could break, and think of yourself the same way: breakable, and carrying something. If you pray, thank God for what you carry; if not, notice how carefully you're holding it.
Earthen vessels. Paul's picture of himself and every Christian: plain clay jars, carrying a treasure that isn't their own. Today's word.
Your line: treasure in clay. Plain jars kept the scrolls safe. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.

578.title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10)
578.hook: a thorn in the flesh, and my grace is sufficient for thee
578.howItsDone: Catholics speak of "offering up" a suffering, uniting it to Christ's; the Church also prays for healing, and offers the anointing of the sick to those who are seriously ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, earthen vessels: Paul and every Christian as plain clay jars. Your line was treasure in clay.

Paul's critics in Corinth liked credentials: visions, revelations, impressive speech. So Paul plays their game, reluctantly. He knows a man, he says, who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven and heard words no one may speak. A few verses on, it's clear the man is Paul himself. It's the kind of story his rivals would have loved to tell. And just as they lean in, Paul stops boasting about visions and starts boasting about something else entirely: a wound he couldn't get rid of.
screen: `CRITICS WHO LIKED CREDENTIALS.` → `CAUGHT UP TO THE THIRD HEAVEN.` → `THEN PAUL BOASTS OF A WOUND.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims he calls it "a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me." The King James calls it a thorn in the flesh. The Greek word, skolops, can mean a splinter or a sharpened stake. What was it? Nobody knows, and Paul never says. Readers have guessed for centuries: an eye disease, since he mentions writing in large letters; malaria; migraines; epilepsy; a stammer; the opponents who dogged him; a temptation he couldn't shake. The silence may be a mercy: anyone can put their own thorn in that space. What Paul does tell us is what he did. Three times he asked the Lord to take it away. The answer was not yes. It was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity." Paul turns the boasting upside down: "Gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me." The Greek for dwell is a word about pitching a tent: Christ's power camps where Paul is weakest. Then the line the whole passage has been building to: "For when I am weak, then am I powerful." Catholics have found company here. Some of the Church's saints lived with illness, pain and limits that never lifted. The Church doesn't call suffering good in itself, and it prays for healing. But it holds that a weakness offered to God is not wasted. The thorn stayed. The grace came with it.

segments.voice: Name, quietly, in a word or two, one weakness you carry that hasn't gone away, however much you've wished it would: a body that hurts, a temper, anxiety, a loss. Don't analyze it or fix it; just notice how heavy it feels. If you pray, say Paul's answer back to God, my grace is sufficient, and stay with it; if not, notice that you're still here, carrying it.

579.title: A cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–8)
579.howItsDone: Catholics give through the parish collection at Mass, through Lenten almsgiving, and through charities such as the Society of St. Vincent de Paul; the Church counts almsgiving among the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, skolops: the thorn that stayed, and the grace that came with it. Your line was my grace is sufficient.

Paul spent years running a collection. Churches of Gentile believers, in Greece and Asia Minor, were asked to put money aside for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He mentions it in Romans and in both letters to Corinth. It was money, and it was also a sign: the newer churches sharing with the mother church that had given them the Gospel. In Second Corinthians he gives the subject a long stretch of the letter. He praises the churches of Macedonia, who gave out of deep poverty, beyond their means. Then he turns to Corinth, which had promised a lot and not yet delivered.
screen: `A COLLECTION FOR JERUSALEM.` → `MACEDONIA GAVE FROM POVERTY.` → `CORINTH HAD PROMISED.`

segments.voice: He starts with a farmer's rule: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will reap generously. Then he says how to give: "Every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." First, decide in your heart. Paul doesn't set an amount. Second, not with sadness: no grudging, no giving while silently resenting it. Third, not of necessity: not squeezed out by pressure or shame. The Greek word for cheerful is hilaros: glad, bright, ready. Paul seems to be echoing a line from the old Greek version of the book of Proverbs, which says God blesses a cheerful giver. Then he adds a promise: God is able to make all grace abound in you, so that you have enough, and enough left over for every good work. In Paul's picture, giving isn't a loss to be endured. It's seed, and God keeps you supplied with more. Catholics put this into practice in many ways. Almsgiving is one of the three traditional practices of Lent, with prayer and fasting. The Catechism counts giving to the poor among the works of mercy and calls it a work of justice pleasing to God. But Paul's interest here is less in the amount than in the face. Two people can put the same money in the basket. One with a sigh. One with a smile. Paul says God loves the second.
screen: `SOW SPARINGLY, REAP SPARINGLY.` · `DECIDED IN YOUR HEART.` · `NOT WITH SADNESS, NOT FORCED.` · `HILAROS: CHEERFUL.` · then, large: `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you could give: money to someone who needs it, your time, a meal, ten minutes of your full attention. Make it small enough to give without a sigh, decide it in your heart now so it isn't squeezed out of you later, and picture your face as you give it. If you pray, offer the gift to God first; if not, just decide, and let yourself be glad about it.
Hilaros. Greek for glad, bright, ready: the kind of giving God loves, decided in the heart, not squeezed out by sadness or pressure. Today's word.

580.title: All one (Galatians 3:26–28)
580.hook: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female
580.howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment as a sign of having put on Christ; the same rite is used for every person, whatever their rank.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hilaros: God loveth a cheerful giver, decided in the heart. Your line was cheerful.

In the story Acts tells, the first followers of Jesus were Jews. Then Gentiles began to believe too, and a hard question split the young movement. Did a Gentile have to become Jewish first, be circumcised and take on the law of Moses, to belong fully? In the churches of Galatia, in what's now central Turkey, teachers were saying yes. Paul, a Jew himself and proud of it, was saying no. The letter to the Galatians is the heat of that argument. And in the middle of it, Paul writes a sentence that still startles.
screen: `JEWS FIRST, THEN GENTILES.` → `MUST THEY BECOME JEWISH FIRST?` → `A STARTLING SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: He starts with what makes someone belong: "For you are all the children of God by faith, in Christ Jesus." Then baptism: "For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ." Put on, like clothing. And then: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus." Those three pairs were lines that divided the world Paul lived in: people, status, sex. Notice the third pair is worded differently from the first two. In the Greek it reads, literally, no male and female: the words of Genesis, where God creates them male and female. Paul is reaching back to creation. And notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the differences vanish. In his letters he still writes to slaves and masters, husbands and wives, Jews and Greeks, as who they are. What he says is that in Christ none of these decides who belongs, or who ranks higher. The word one, in Greek, is masculine: not one thing, a blend, but one person, as if all of them together were one new man in Christ. Catholics see this at the font. In the rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment, a sign that they have put on Christ. A child, an elderly convert, a prince, a refugee: the same water, the same white cloth. Christians have taken centuries, and are still taking them, to live out what this sentence says.
screen: `CHILDREN OF GOD BY FAITH.` · `BAPTIZED: YOU HAVE PUT ON CHRIST.` · `NO MALE AND FEMALE: GENESIS.` · `ONE: NOT A BLEND, ONE PERSON.` · then, large: `YOU ARE ALL ONE IN CHRIST JESUS.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you'll see today: at home, at work, on the bus, the person who serves your coffee. Notice, without scolding yourself, who you put higher and who you barely see, then picture them all in the same white garment, at the same font. If you pray, pray for the ones you usually overlook; if not, hold them all in the same light for a moment.
All one. Paul's sentence to the Galatians: neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, but all one in Christ Jesus. Today's word.

581.title: The fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23)
581.hook: the Latin Bible lists twelve: charity, joy, peace, patience and more (CCC 1832)
581.howItsDone: Catholics learn the twelve fruits of the Spirit as listed in the Catechism (1832), often in preparation for confirmation, alongside the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all one: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female. Your line was all one in christ.

Open a modern Bible to Galatians chapter five and count the fruit of the Spirit. Nine. Now open the Douay-Rheims to the same verse and count again. Twelve. Nobody slipped in a few extra. The difference is centuries old, and it says something about how the Bible traveled. Paul has just listed what he calls the works of the flesh: enmities, contentions, envy, anger, quarrels, drunkenness and more. Now he lists the opposite, and the Catholic Church still counts it the old way.
screen: `NINE IN ONE BIBLE.` → `TWELVE IN ANOTHER.` → `THE WORKS OF THE FLESH, THEN THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "But the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity." Twelve. The Greek text behind modern Bibles has nine. The old Latin Bible has twelve; some scholars think early translators rendered a few Greek words with two Latin ones. The Catechism lists the twelve, and says that the tradition of the Church counts them so. Look at two words Paul chose. First, works versus fruit. Works are things you make: you build them, you produce them. Fruit grows. You can water a tree and prune it, but you can't force an apple. Paul's point is that these qualities are what the Spirit grows in a life given over to God. Second, fruit, not fruits. In Paul's Greek it's singular, one fruit, the way one orange has many segments. Charity heads the list, and the others may be read as its flavors. Today's line comes from Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, talking about telling true teachers from false: "By their fruits you shall know them." A tree is known by what it bears. Catholics use the twelve as a kind of mirror. Not a checklist to grade yourself, but a way to notice what's already growing. And the list is very ordinary. Patience in traffic. Mildness on the phone. Joy at a kitchen table. Nothing on it requires a miracle, just a life where something is quietly growing.
screen: `TWELVE IN LATIN, NINE IN GREEK.` · `WORKS ARE MADE, FRUIT GROWS.` · `ONE FRUIT, MANY FLAVORS.` · `KNOWN BY WHAT IT BEARS.` · then, large: `BY THEIR FRUITS YOU SHALL KNOW THEM.`

segments.voice: Let the list pass slowly through your mind: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long patience, mildness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Don't grade yourself; just ask which one you've actually seen in yourself this week, even once, even small, and remember the scene. If you pray, thank God for what's growing; if not, notice it and be glad.
Karpos. The Greek word for fruit, singular: one fruit of the Spirit with many flavors, charity first among them. Today's word.
Your line: by their fruits. And that's week eighty-three: enigma, where is thy sting, earthen vessels, skolops, a cheerful giver, all one, and the fruits of the Spirit. Until tomorrow.
